turns.t: Good afternoon, doctor. I was told to come for my follow-up after losing the baby, three weeks on from the hospital.
Good afternoon, do sit down. I'm very sorry for what you've been through. How have you been coping, in yourself?
Oh, one gets on with it, thank you. My husband has been marvellous, he's even taken up cooking.
Has he? What's his signature dish?
Cheese on toast, I'm afraid. Burnt, mostly. But it's the thought that counts.
Quite right. Now, tell me about the body side of things. Anything bothering you at the moment?
There's some cramping low down, like period pains, mainly in the evenings.
When did the cramping begin? Was it straight after you came home?
Goodness, I really couldn't say. It might have been the week after, or perhaps before, it's all rather a blur.
That's completely understandable. Anything else?
I've been terribly tired, for about three weeks. I'm in bed by eight, which is not like me at all.
Mm. Have you had any fever or shivers since you came home?
No, no fever at all. I did check, because the nurse at the ward told me to.
Good, that's what I wanted to hear. Do you have any history of operations I should know about?
Only my appendix, taken out when I was fifteen. Nothing since.
And anyone in the family with gynaecological trouble? Mother, sisters?
My mother had fibroids, if that's relevant. She never really spoke about it.
It's worth knowing, thank you. Now, forgive me, I must ask about allergies. Any to medicines or anything else?
Well, that's the odd thing. I think I might be allergic to something they gave me in hospital, but nobody could tell me what.
Do you remember what happened when you took it?
I felt dreadful for an hour or so, and the nurse made a note. Then everyone went rather vague about it.
I see. So we have a possible allergy, no name, no clear reaction. I'll ask the hospital to send their notes, but let's be careful in the meantime.
Yes please. I'd hate to make a fuss, but I'd rather know.
Not a fuss at all. Right, would you like a chaperone for the examination? Our healthcare assistant is just outside.
Yes, that would be kind.
Hello there, I'm Priya. I'll just stand by the curtain, shout if you need anything.
Thank you, Priya. Lovely to meet you.
Lie back for me and let your knees relax. I'm pressing gently on your tummy now. Tell me if it's sore.
That's fine, doctor. Just a bit strange having it pressed.
The abdomen feels soft, and there's no tenderness in the lower right side.
All finished. You can sit up whenever you're ready. Priya, thanks, that's all.
No problem, doctor. I'll leave you to it. Take care, love.
Goodbye, and thank you again.
Now, what I'm seeing and hearing is most likely a womb that's settling back down normally. The cramps fit with that.
That is a relief. I had imagined all sorts.
The tiredness is common too, but I'd like to give you iron tablets. Ferrous sulfate 200 mg twice a day, with a little orange juice if you can bear it.
Orange juice I can manage. The cheese on toast may be harder.
Ha. Tea can block the iron, so keep your cuppa away from the tablets by an hour or so.
Gosh, that's going to be the hard part. Is it all right to carry on walking in the garden?
Gentle walks are good for you. Go at your own pace and rest when you need to.
Wonderful. My roses need me, you see. I've been neglecting them dreadfully.
What sort do you grow?
Mostly old English roses. Tea scented, and a few climbers that have gone rather wild.
Lovely. Do keep some energy for the rest of life as well. And if you ever feel you want to talk to someone, tell us.
That's very good to know, thank you. I may well do that.
Any other questions before you go?
No, I think you've covered everything. You've been very kind, doctor.
Look after yourself. The prescription will be at the front desk on your way out.
Marvellous. Goodbye, then.
Goodbye, and mind the step by the door.
